vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: a short informal meeting to hear what is new
the area of the world that shares the same clock time
the person with the same role in another country
used to add something that is not the main subject
a work meeting held away from the office
to start talking more freely about something
the amount of work a person or a team has
to make short contact with somebody to check something

tips: Busy, in a good way. We closed the audit this week. How about you?
One detail, then return the question.

items.situation: He says he has been travelling for three weeks.
tips: That sounds challenging with the time zones. Do you manage to keep your catch-ups?

items.situation: She mentions a reorganisation in her team.
tips: Speaking of which, how is that working on your side?
speaking of which connects to what she just said.

items.situation: You want to ask about the November offsite.
tips: By the way, are you coming to the offsite in November?
by the way opens a light new subject.

items.situation: You want a short contact next month.
tips: Let us touch base in October about the visit.
touch base = short contact, not a long meeting.

items.situation: You want to propose a regular short meeting.
tips: Shall we have a catch-up every two weeks, thirty minutes?
catch-up as a noun, with a hyphen.

listenings.text: Camila, hi, good to see you. We have a few minutes before the others join, so tell me, how are things on your side? Things here have changed quite a lot, actually. My team was reorganised in April. Two business units became one, and now I cover both, which is interesting and also a lot. The time difference with you is five hours, and honestly that is the hardest part of my week, so I try to start these calls early in my afternoon. Anyway, I wanted to ask you something before the agenda. Would you like to have a short catch-up every two weeks? Thirty minutes, no agenda, just to hear what is happening in your region. I find that I learn more in those thirty minutes than in the monthly committee.

Let me show you the other version of the same five minutes. I open the call and I ask, how are things on your side? And the answer comes back: fine, thanks. That is all. So I try again. I ask, how is the new process working in your region? And the answer is: it is working well. Again, two seconds. After that we both look at the screen and wait for the others to join, and nobody learns anything. Nothing there was rude and nothing was wrong. The English was correct. But those five minutes before the agenda are where you find out what is really happening in another region, and where the other person finds out that they can call you when something is difficult. It is the cheapest thirty seconds of relationship you will ever buy.
